comments.author: @DorritHansen
comments.text: Is the proved origin of the walrus ivory in the walrus populations further north not establishing the connection and the length of the period involved?

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Yes, it does establish an important connection. The genomic evidence shows that part of the Norse ivory supply came from High Arctic walrus populations near Baffin Island. What it can’t tell us by itself is whether those hunters actually landed on Baffin, used a specific site like Tanfield Valley, or how long they may have stayed there. That’s the missing archaeological link the video is getting at.

comments.text:

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: Definitely long before Columbus 😄 The evidence points to people being in the Americas far earlier than 5,000 years ago, at least around 15,000 years ago, and possibly earlier. Some migrations likely followed coastal routes and may have involved watercraft, while others came through Beringia. The exact routes are still debated. As for Foo Man Choo running the first passenger service… I think that part might need a little more archaeology 😂

comments.text: Why should they,the klima in Norway at the 60°N latitude when they heading west got colder as they touched the southern tip of the Shetland isles,the southern tip of Greenland and the northeastern tip of the main North Americas mainland at Mt.Torngat,these three points of land makes the safest travel at 60°N latitude before anyone knew about Iceland. Its an insult to our common sense as norsemen. Grr😢😅

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: That’s a fair point, the Norse were not randomly wandering into the unknown with no sense of weather, currents, or safer stepping-stone routes. They knew how to use landfalls, latitude, and seasonal conditions better than we often give them credit for. The tricky part is that archaeology can only prove where we have physical evidence, not every route that made sense to experienced sailors. So I agree the voyage was absolutely plausible, the question is just where the proof survived.

comments.author: @jefftaylor529
comments.text: What is frustrating to me is, considering settlements further south as mentioned in the Sagas, there may never be evidence found to prove the location of Straumfjord as the coast has been so over-developed over the centuries..

replies.author: @jefftaylor529
replies.text: ​@HiddenCanadathe strong currents could be attributed to the Bay of Fundy as well. In a broader sense, with Greenlanders inhabiting that land until the 14th century they realistically needed wood and thus a place they could continuously get it from.. so logic would tell us there's much more to be discovered in the Maritimes and New England..

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: I’d be cautious about placing Straumfjord too confidently anywhere, but Buzzards Bay is definitely one of the more interesting southern candidates. The sagas describe a place with strong currents and nearby islands, so people have proposed everything from the Gulf of St. Lawrence to Maine and even parts of coastal Massachusetts. My personal view is that L’Anse aux Meadows was probably the base camp, while the more southern saga locations may have been resource areas the Norse reached but didn’t leave much behind. Buzzards Bay fits parts of the description, but without archaeology, it stays in that frustrating “possible but unproven” category.

replies.author: @jefftaylor529
replies.text: ​@HiddenCanadado you have any opinion to share on how far south Straumfjord might be? I am on Buzzards Bay and I do know it is listed as one possible location as described in the Sagas themselves.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: That’s a really good point. Coastal development may have erased or buried a lot of the evidence we’d need, especially for places like Straumfjord that are still tied more to saga geography than confirmed archaeology. That’s what makes this whole mystery so frustrating, the sagas may be pointing somewhere real, but the physical proof may be gone, hidden, or sitting under modern development.
